opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that human cognition is fundamentally grounded in our interaction with a physical world. Everything we understand, even our most abstract concepts, is ultimately built on a foundation of embodied experience. As infants we learn about objects by grasping them and watching them fall. We learn that things persist when they're out of sight, that solid objects can't pass through each other, that we can push and pull and stack things. That's what I'd call a kind of everyday physics, or common sense, and it underpins an enormous amount of what we do cognitively.

Then think about language. When we use words like "grasp" an idea, or "support" an argument, or talk about something being "over" or "behind" us in time, those metaphors are rooted in bodily experience of space and movement. So the meanings of words aren't free-floating symbols. They connect back, ultimately, to this shared embodied world that we all inhabit together.

Now, a disembodied system, say something trained purely on text, encounters only the traces of all that. It sees how words relate to other words, and it can pick up an astonishing amount from that, frankly more than many of us expected. But there's a real question about whether it has the same kind of grounding. Does it understand that a cup will spill if you tip it, in the way that you or I do, or does it just know that the word "spill" tends to co-occur with "tip" and "cup"? Often the behaviour looks the same, but the difference shows up at the edges, in novel situations where you have to reason from a genuine model of how the world works rather than from statistical patterns in descriptions of it.

I'd add a social dimension too. We're embodied among other embodied creatures. So much of our cognition is about other agents, their intentions, their perspectives, what they can see and what they can't. That develops through interacting with others in a shared physical space, through joint attention and so on.

So I wouldn't say it's impossible to build a disembodied system with very impressive capabilities. Clearly we can. But I'd be cautious about the idea that you can get the full package of human-like general intelligence, with that robust common sense and that flexible understanding, without something playing the role that embodiment plays for us. Whether that has to be literal physical embodiment, or whether rich interaction with a simulated or virtual world might suffice, is a very interesting open question.

r001.rationale: It says people learn about objects by interacting with them and observing what happens, and describes this as building a model of how the world works.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of physical properties and everyday physics but does not describe discontinuities against spatial smoothness.

r003.rationale: It says common sense is built on embodied experience and describes everyday physical regularities—such as objects falling, persisting, and resisting passage—as its foundation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that a great deal of what we think of as human cognition is really built on top of our being embodied creatures, situated in a physical world full of objects, and interacting with other embodied creatures. If you look at the way human concepts are structured, even quite abstract ones, they tend to be grounded in our bodily experience. We talk about "grasping" an idea, or being "under" pressure, or "moving forward" with a plan. There's a long tradition in cognitive science, people like Lakoff and Johnson, pointing out that our abstract thought is shot through with metaphors drawn from sensorimotor experience, from having a body that moves around in space and pushes things and gets pushed back.

So the worry is that if you take a system that's only ever had access to text, or to some very impoverished channel of interaction with the world, then even if it manages to reproduce the surface form of human language very convincingly, there may be a sense in which it doesn't really understand what it's talking about, because the understanding, for us, bottoms out in something like knowing what it's like to manipulate an object, or what happens when you drop something, or how another agent's behaviour is going to unfold in front of you. There's a kind of common-sense physics and common-sense psychology that we acquire in infancy, through interaction, and I've long argued that this common sense is actually the hard core of the problem of human-level intelligence.

Now, I should say I'm a bit less dogmatic about this than I used to be. Large language models have surprised me. They've been trained on so much text that the text itself encodes an enormous amount of the structure of the world, second hand, as it were. So they can exhibit a surprising degree of apparently sensible reasoning about physical situations without ever having had a body. But I think there's still a question about how robust that is, and whether it would generalise the way it does in a creature that has actually had to cope with the world. A disembodied system has never had to care about anything in the way that an animal has to care about not falling off a cliff, or finding food, and that kind of embeddedness, that stake in the world, may turn out to be rather deeply woven into what cognition is for us. So I'd say it's not impossible in principle to build a disembodied system with human-like capabilities, but it's working against the grain of how those capabilities actually arose.

r001.rationale: The response says common-sense physics is acquired through interaction and grounds understanding in learning how objects behave, such as what happens when something is dropped.

r002.rationale: It mentions moving through space and physical objects, but does not describe discontinuities in the physical world against spatial smoothness.

r003.rationale: It grounds common-sense physics and psychology in infancy’s interactions with the world and in bodily experience of objects and other agents.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the difficulty is that our cognitive capabilities are deeply bound up with being embodied creatures. We encounter the world through perception and action, and we learn about it by doing things. We move around, manipulate objects, and discover how things respond. That gives our concepts a grounding that a purely disembodied system would have to acquire somehow by other means.

And we’re social creatures as well. A great deal of human understanding develops through interacting with other people, attending to the same things, and learning what matters to one another. Language sits within that broader context of shared activity.

So I wouldn’t say that embodiment is necessarily a prerequisite for intelligence. But if the aim is to replicate human cognitive capabilities, then removing the body also removes a substantial part of the machinery through which those capabilities develop. The question is what you would put in its place.

r001.rationale: The response says people learn about the world through action and manipulation, discovering how things respond; this communicates learning physical cause-and-effect through embodied interaction.

r002.rationale: It does not describe spatial smoothness or discontinuities in the everyday physical world.

r003.rationale: It says physical interaction grounds concepts, but does not clearly identify regularities of physical interaction as the basis for foundational common-sense concepts.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the difficulty is that human cognition is very deeply bound up with being embodied. We encounter the world through perception and action, and what we learn is shaped by the things we can do, the things we need, and the consequences of our actions. So our concepts aren’t acquired in isolation; they’re part of that ongoing interaction with the world.

If you build a disembodied system, you’re taking away a great deal of the structure that supports human learning. You then have to ask what replaces it. How does the system acquire an understanding of cause and effect, or distinguish what matters from what doesn’t?

That doesn’t mean a disembodied system couldn’t be intelligent, or even reproduce many human capabilities. But we shouldn’t assume that we can separate human cognition from the circumstances in which it develops and expect the same capacities to emerge.

r001.rationale: The response says human learning is shaped by perception, action, and their consequences, and asks how a disembodied system would acquire cause-and-effect understanding.

r002.rationale: It does not describe discontinuities in the everyday physical world against spatial smoothness.

r003.rationale: It links concepts broadly to ongoing interaction, but does not ground foundational common-sense concepts in regularities of physical interaction.
